name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Types of intermolecular forces and interacting species

questiontext.text:
Match the intermolecular interactions in List I with the nature of interacting particles in List II.

List I (Interaction)List II (Interacting Particles)
(A) Dispersion forces(i) Molecules with permanent dipoles
(B) Dipole–dipole forces(ii) Polar molecule and nonpolar molecule
(C) Dipole–induced dipole forces(iii) Molecules with N–H, O–H, or H–F bonds
(D) Hydrogen bonding(iv) Atoms and nonpolar molecules

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intermolecular forces arise from electrostatic interactions between partial or transient charges on atoms and molecules.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Interaction
Dispersion (London) forces occur between electrically symmetrical atoms and nonpolar molecules due to instantaneous and induced dipoles. Dipole–dipole forces act between molecules possessing permanent dipoles. Dipole–induced dipole forces operate between a polar molecule with a permanent dipole and a nonpolar molecule. Hydrogen bonding is a strong special case of dipole–dipole interaction found in molecules containing highly polar \(\text{N–H}\), \(\text{O–H}\), or \(\text{H–F}\) bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct pairings are: dispersion forces with atoms and nonpolar molecules; dipole–dipole forces with molecules having permanent dipoles; dipole–induced dipole forces with a polar molecule and a nonpolar molecule; and hydrogen bonding with molecules containing \(\text{N–H}\), \(\text{O–H}\), or \(\text{H–F}\) bonds, corresponding to A–iv, B–i, C–ii, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Ideal gas laws and their mathematical expressions

questiontext.text:
Match the gas laws in List I with their corresponding mathematical relationships and constant parameters in List II.

List I (Gas Law)List II (Relation and Constants)
(A) Boyle's law(i) \(V \propto T\) at constant \(p\) and \(n\)
(B) Charles' law(ii) \(V \propto n\) at constant \(T\) and \(p\)
(C) Gay-Lussac's law(iii) \(p \propto \frac{1}{V}\) at constant \(T\) and \(n\)
(D) Avogadro law(iv) \(p \propto T\) at constant \(V\) and \(n\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each ideal gas law relates two state variables among pressure \(p\), volume \(V\), absolute temperature \(T\), and number of moles \(n\) while holding the remaining two variables constant.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Law
Boyle's law states that pressure varies inversely with volume (\(p \propto \frac{1}{V}\)) at constant \(T\) and \(n\). Charles' law states that volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (\(V \propto T\)) at constant \(p\) and \(n\). Gay-Lussac's law states that pressure varies directly with absolute temperature (\(p \propto T\)) at constant \(V\) and \(n\). Avogadro law states that volume is directly proportional to the number of moles (\(V \propto n\)) at constant \(T\) and \(p\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Gas law plots and their characteristic names

questiontext.text:
Match the graphical plots in List I with their correct descriptions in List II.

List I (Plot)List II (Description)
(A) \(p\) vs \(V\) at constant \(T\)(i) Isochore
(B) \(V\) vs \(t\,(^\circ\mathrm{C})\) at constant \(p\)(ii) Horizontal line at \(Z = 1\)
(C) \(p\) vs \(T\,(\mathrm{K})\) at constant \(V\)(iii) Isotherm
(D) \(Z\) vs \(p\) for an ideal gas(iv) Isobar

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Graphs of gas behaviour held at constant temperature, constant pressure, or constant volume are named after the parameter kept fixed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Plot
A \(p\) versus \(V\) plot at constant temperature is called an isotherm. A \(V\) versus Celsius temperature plot at constant pressure is called an isobar. A \(p\) versus Kelvin temperature plot at constant volume is called an isochore. For an ideal gas, \(Z = \frac{pV}{nRT} = 1\) at all pressures, giving a horizontal straight line parallel to the pressure axis at \(Z = 1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Distance dependence and energy of intermolecular interactions

questiontext.text:
Match the intermolecular interactions in List I with their energy characteristics in List II.

List I (Interaction)List II (Energy Characteristic)
(A) Dispersion (London) force(i) Interaction energy \(\propto \frac{1}{r^3}\)
(B) Dipole–dipole interaction (stationary polar molecules)(ii) Energy ranges from \(10\) to \(100\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(C) Dipole–dipole interaction (rotating polar molecules)(iii) Important only at short distances (\(\sim 500\text{ pm}\)), energy \(\propto \frac{1}{r^6}\)
(D) Hydrogen bond(iv) Interaction energy \(\propto \frac{1}{r^6}\) between permanent dipoles

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The interaction energy of intermolecular attractions decays with intermolecular separation \(r\) at different rates depending on whether dipoles are permanent, rotating, or induced.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Interaction
Dispersion (London) forces are important only at short distances (\(\sim 500\text{ pm}\)) with interaction energy proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^6}\). Dipole–dipole interaction energy between stationary polar molecules (as in solids) is proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^3}\), whereas between rotating polar molecules it is proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^6}\). The energy of a hydrogen bond varies between \(10\) and \(100\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Standard molar volumes and universal gas constant values

questiontext.text:
Match the gas constants and standard molar volumes in List I with their numerical values in List II.

List I (Quantity)List II (Value)
(A) Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (\(273.15\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\))(i) \(8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
(B) Molar volume of an ideal gas at SATP (\(298.15\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\))(ii) \(22.71\text{ L mol}^{-1}\)
(C) Universal gas constant \(R\) in SI units(iii) \(8.20578 \times 10^{-2}\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
(D) Universal gas constant \(R\) in \(\text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)(iv) \(24.789\text{ L mol}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard temperature and pressure (STP) is defined as \(273.15\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\) (\(10^5\text{ Pa}\)), while standard ambient temperature and pressure (SATP) is \(298.15\text{ K}\) and \(1\text{ bar}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the ideal gas equation, \(V_m = \frac{RT}{p}\) and \(R = \frac{pV}{nT}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
At STP (\(273.15\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\)), the molar volume of an ideal gas is \(22.71\text{ L mol}^{-1}\). At SATP (\(298.15\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\)), the molar volume is \(24.789\text{ L mol}^{-1}\). Calculating \(R\) in SI units gives \(8.314\text{ Pa m}^3\text{ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 8.314\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Using \(1\text{ atm}\) and \(22.414\text{ L mol}^{-1}\) at \(273.15\text{ K}\) gives \(R = 8.20578 \times 10^{-2}\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Liquid state physical properties and SI units

questiontext.text:
Match the liquid-state quantities in List I with their corresponding SI units in List II.

List I (Quantity)List II (SI Unit)
(A) Surface tension (\(\gamma\))(i) \(\text{J m}^{-2}\)
(B) Surface energy(ii) \(\text{Pa s}\)
(C) Coefficient of viscosity (\(\eta\))(iii) \(\text{s}^{-1}\)
(D) Velocity gradient (\(\frac{du}{dz}\))(iv) \(\text{N m}^{-1}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each physical quantity in the liquid state has a characteristic SI unit derived from its defining equation.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Evaluation
Surface tension \(\gamma\) is the force acting per unit length perpendicular to a line on the liquid surface, so its SI unit is \(\text{N m}^{-1}\) (\(\text{kg s}^{-2}\)). Surface energy is the energy required to increase surface area by one unit, giving \(\text{J m}^{-2}\). Coefficient of viscosity \(\eta\) from \(F = \eta A \frac{du}{dz}\) has SI unit \(\text{N s m}^{-2} = \text{Pa s}\). Velocity gradient \(\frac{du}{dz}\) has dimensions of velocity divided by distance, \(\frac{\text{m s}^{-1}}{\text{m}} = \text{s}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iv, B–i, C–ii, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Molecular speeds and kinetic energy expressions

questiontext.text:
Match the kinetic theory terms in List I with their corresponding definitions or mathematical expressions in List II.

List I (Term)List II (Definition / Expression)
(A) Most probable speed (\(u_{\text{mp}}\))(i) \(\frac{1}{2}m\overline{u^2}\)
(B) Root mean square speed (\(u_{\text{rms}}\))(ii) \(1 : 1.128 : 1.224\)
(C) Average translational kinetic energy(iii) Speed possessed by maximum number of molecules
(D) Ratio \(u_{\text{mp}} : u_{\text{av}} : u_{\text{rms}}\)(iv) \(\sqrt{\overline{u^2}}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds, different statistical averages characterize molecular motion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
The most probable speed \(u_{\text{mp}}\) is the speed corresponding to the peak of the distribution curve, i.e., possessed by the maximum number of molecules. The root mean square speed \(u_{\text{rms}}\) is the square root of the mean of the squares of speeds, \(\sqrt{\overline{u^2}}\). Average translational kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2}m\overline{u^2}\). The three speeds are related by the ratio \(u_{\text{mp}} : u_{\text{av}} : u_{\text{rms}} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - van der Waals parameters and compressibility factor

questiontext.text:
Match the real-gas parameters in List I with their physical significance or expressions in List II.

List I (Parameter)List II (Significance / Expression)
(A) van der Waals constant \(a\)(i) \(\frac{V_{\text{real}}}{V_{\text{ideal}}}\)
(B) Volume correction \(nb\)(ii) \(\frac{an^2}{V^2}\)
(C) Pressure correction term(iii) Measure of magnitude of intermolecular attractive forces
(D) Compressibility factor \(Z\)(iv) Approximate total volume occupied by the gas molecules

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The van der Waals equation \(\left(p + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT\) modifies the ideal gas equation for intermolecular attractions and finite molecular volume.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Parameter
The van der Waals constant \(a\) measures the magnitude of intermolecular attractive forces within the gas. The term \(nb\) represents the approximate total volume occupied by the gas molecules themselves, restricting free motion to \((V - nb)\). The pressure correction term added to observed pressure is \(\frac{an^2}{V^2}\). The compressibility factor \(Z = \frac{pV_{\text{real}}}{nRT}\) simplifies to \(\frac{V_{\text{real}}}{V_{\text{ideal}}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–ii, D–i.

questiontext.text:
Match the substances in List I with their critical temperatures (\(T_c\)) in List II.

List I (Substance)List II (Critical Temperature, \(T_c\))
(A) \(\mathrm{He}\)(i) \(304.10\text{ K}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{H_2}\)(ii) \(647.1\text{ K}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)(iii) \(5.3\text{ K}\)
(D) \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)(iv) \(33.2\text{ K}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Critical temperature \(T_c\) increases with the strength of intermolecular attractive forces between particles of a substance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Substance
Helium (\(\mathrm{He}\)) has the weakest dispersion forces and the lowest critical temperature, \(5.3\text{ K}\). Dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)) has slightly stronger interactions with \(T_c = 33.2\text{ K}\). Carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)) has \(T_c = 304.10\text{ K}\) (\(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)). Water (\(\mathrm{H_2O}\)) exhibits strong hydrogen bonding, giving the highest critical temperature among these at \(647.1\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Normal boiling points of common liquids

questiontext.text:
Match the liquids in List I with their normal boiling points (at \(760\text{ mm Hg}\)) in List II.

List I (Liquid)List II (Normal Boiling Point)
(A) Diethyl ether(i) \(373\text{ K}\)
(B) Carbon tetrachloride(ii) \(308\text{ K}\)
(C) Ethyl alcohol(iii) \(351.3\text{ K}\)
(D) Water(iv) \(349.7\text{ K}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The normal boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals \(1\text{ atm}\) (\(760\text{ mm Hg}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Liquid
From the vapour pressure versus temperature curves, diethyl ether is the most volatile and reaches \(760\text{ mm Hg}\) at \(308\text{ K}\). Carbon tetrachloride has a normal boiling point of \(349.7\text{ K}\), slightly lower than that of ethyl alcohol at \(351.3\text{ K}\). Water has the lowest vapour pressure at a given temperature and boils at \(373\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the correct matching is A–ii, B–iv, C–iii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q11 - Liquid phenomena and governing physical properties

questiontext.text:
Match the observed phenomena in List I with the governing liquid-state property or principle in List II.

List I (Phenomenon)List II (Governing Property / Principle)
(A) Fire polishing of sharp glass edges(i) Extremely high viscosity
(B) Use of pressure cooker at high altitudes(ii) Capillary rise due to surface tension
(C) Rise of liquid in a thin glass capillary(iii) Boiling point increases with external pressure
(D) Solid-like behaviour of glass(iv) Liquid surface rounds off to minimise surface area

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Macroscopic behaviour of liquids such as droplet shape, capillary action, boiling point shifts, and flow resistance are governed by vapour pressure, surface tension, and viscosity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Phenomenon
During fire polishing, heated glass melts and surface tension pulls the liquid surface into a rounded shape to minimise surface area. At high altitudes, water boils at a lower temperature because atmospheric pressure is low; a pressure cooker raises external pressure to increase the boiling point. Rise of a liquid in a thin capillary is driven by surface tension. Glass is an extremely viscous liquid whose high viscosity causes many properties to resemble solids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iv, B–iii, C–ii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q12 - Compressibility factor Z across pressure and temperature regimes

questiontext.text:
Match the pressure and temperature conditions for a real gas in List I with the corresponding compressibility factor \(Z\) behaviour in List II.

List I (Condition)List II (Behaviour of \(Z\))
(A) Very low pressure (\(p \to 0\))(i) \(Z > 1\) across all positive pressures
(B) Very high pressure for any real gas(ii) \(Z < 1\) reaching a minimum
(C) Below Boyle temperature at intermediate pressure(iii) \(Z = 1\) (ideal behaviour)
(D) Above Boyle temperature(iv) \(Z > 1\); gas is more difficult to compress

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The compressibility factor \(Z = \frac{pV}{nRT} = \frac{V_{\text{real}}}{V_{\text{ideal}}}\) measures deviation from ideal gas behaviour across different pressure and temperature regimes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
When pressure approaches zero (\(p \to 0\)), molecules are far apart and intermolecular interactions are negligible, so \(Z = 1\). At very high pressures, molecular volume and repulsive forces dominate for all real gases, giving \(Z > 1\) and lower compressibility than an ideal gas. Below the Boyle temperature at intermediate pressures, attractive forces dominate and \(Z\) decreases below \(1\) to a minimum. Above the Boyle temperature, attractive forces are very feeble and real gases show positive deviation (\(Z > 1\)) across positive pressures.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–ii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q13 - Andrews isotherms of CO2 and phase regions

questiontext.text:
Match the regions or points on Thomas Andrews' \(p\)–\(V\) isotherms of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in List I with their physical interpretation in List II.

List I (Region / Point)List II (Physical Interpretation)
(A) Isotherm above \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)(i) Liquid and gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexist in equilibrium
(B) Point at \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(73\text{ atm}\)(ii) Compression of liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (very low compressibility)
(C) Horizontal portion inside the dome below \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)(iii) Single-phase fluid; cannot be liquefied by pressure alone
(D) Steep nearly vertical curve to the left of the dome(iv) Critical point where the liquid–vapour boundary disappears

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Andrews' isotherms for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) show the continuity between gaseous and liquid states and define the critical constants \(T_c = 30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(p_c = 73\text{ atm}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Region or Point
Above \(T_c = 30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) remains a single-phase fluid and cannot be liquefied regardless of pressure. At \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(73\text{ atm}\) (the critical point), the horizontal two-phase region merges into a single point and the surface separating liquid and gas disappears. Inside the dome below \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), the horizontal plateau represents liquid and gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexisting in equilibrium at constant pressure. To the left of the dome, the steep line shows that a slight volume decrease causes a sharp pressure rise, representing compression of the nearly incompressible liquid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

questiontext.text:
Match the gas-law problems in List I with their calculated results in List II. (Take \(R = 0.083\text{ bar dm}^3\text{ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\) and STP as \(273\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\)).

List I (Problem)List II (Result)
(A) Final volume when \(2.27\text{ L}\) of a gas at \(1\text{ bar}\) expands to \(0.2\text{ bar}\) at constant \(T\)(i) \(50\text{ K}\)
(B) Partial pressure of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) when \(x_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 0.21\) and \(p_{\text{Total}} = 25\text{ bar}\)(ii) \(3.0\text{ g dm}^{-3}\)
(C) Temperature of \(4.0\text{ mol}\) of an ideal gas occupying \(5\text{ dm}^3\) at \(3.32\text{ bar}\)(iii) \(11.35\text{ L}\)
(D) Density at STP of a gas whose density is \(5.46\text{ g dm}^{-3}\) at \(27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(2\text{ bar}\)(iv) \(5.25\text{ bar}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Relevant Formulae
We use Boyle's law \(p_1V_1 = p_2V_2\), Dalton's law \(p_i = x_i p_{\text{Total}}\), the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\), and the density relation \(d = \frac{pM}{RT}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculations
For the isothermal expansion, \(V_2 = \frac{p_1V_1}{p_2} = \frac{1\text{ bar} \times 2.27\text{ L}}{0.2\text{ bar}} = 11.35\text{ L}\). For the partial pressure of \(\mathrm{O_2}\), \(p_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 0.21 \times 25\text{ bar} = 5.25\text{ bar}\). For the ideal gas temperature, \(T = \frac{pV}{nR} = \frac{3.32 \times 5}{4.0 \times 0.083} = \frac{16.6}{0.332} = 50\text{ K}\). For the gas density at STP (\(273\text{ K}, 1\text{ bar}\)) from \(27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) (\(300\text{ K}\)) and \(2\text{ bar}\), \(d_{\text{STP}} = d_1 \times \frac{p_{\text{STP}}}{p_1} \times \frac{T_1}{T_{\text{STP}}} = 5.46 \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{300}{273} = 3.0\text{ g dm}^{-3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hence, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q15 - Gas mixtures and Daltons law numericals

questiontext.text:
Match the gas mixture systems in List I with their calculated pressure or mole fraction in List II. (Take \(R = 0.083\text{ bar dm}^3\text{ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}\), molar masses: \(\mathrm{H_2} = 2\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)).

List I (System)List II (Calculated Value)
(A) Pressure of dry gas when moist gas at \(293.15\text{ K}\) has \(p_{\text{Total}} = 1.0230\text{ bar}\) (aqueous tension \(= 0.0230\text{ bar}\))(i) \(56.025\text{ bar}\)
(B) Total pressure of \(8\text{ g}\;\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(4\text{ g}\;\mathrm{H_2}\) in \(1\text{ dm}^3\) at \(27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)(ii) \(1.8\text{ bar}\)
(C) Total pressure when \(0.5\text{ L}\;\mathrm{H_2}\) at \(0.8\text{ bar}\) and \(2.0\text{ L}\;\mathrm{O_2}\) at \(0.7\text{ bar}\) are mixed in a \(1\text{ L}\) vessel at \(27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)(iii) \(0.80\)
(D) Mole fraction of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) in a mixture of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) containing \(20\%\) by weight of \(\mathrm{H_2}\)(iv) \(1.0000\text{ bar}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Relevant Formulae
We apply \(p_{\text{Dry gas}} = p_{\text{Total}} - \text{Aqueous tension}\), \(p_{\text{Total}} = (n_1 + n_2)\frac{RT}{V}\), \(p_{\text{Total}}V_{\text{final}} = p_1V_1 + p_2V_2\) at constant \(T\), and \(x_1 = \frac{n_1}{n_1 + n_2}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculations
For the moist gas, \(p_{\text{Dry gas}} = 1.0230 - 0.0230 = 1.0000\text{ bar}\). For \(8\text{ g}\;\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(0.25\text{ mol}\)) and \(4\text{ g}\;\mathrm{H_2}\) (\(2\text{ mol}\)) in \(1\text{ dm}^3\) at \(300\text{ K}\), \(p_{\text{Total}} = \frac{(0.25 + 2.0) \times 0.083 \times 300}{1} = 56.025\text{ bar}\). Mixing \(0.5\text{ L}\) \(\mathrm{H_2}\) at \(0.8\text{ bar}\) and \(2.0\text{ L}\) \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at \(0.7\text{ bar}\) into \(1\text{ L}\) at constant temperature gives \(p_{\text{Total}} = \frac{0.5 \times 0.8 + 2.0 \times 0.7}{1} = 0.4 + 1.4 = 1.8\text{ bar}\). For \(20\text{ g}\;\mathrm{H_2}\) (\(10\text{ mol}\)) and \(80\text{ g}\;\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(2.5\text{ mol}\)), \(x_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{10}{10 + 2.5} = 0.80\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iv, B–i, C–ii, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_MATCHING_MCQ_Q16 - Kinetic theory breakdown and dimensional analysis

questiontext.text:
Match the real-gas concepts in List I with the corresponding statement or unit in List II.

List I (Concept)List II (Statement / Unit)
(A) Kinetic-theory assumption that fails at very high pressure(i) \(p_{\text{ideal}} = p_{\text{real}} + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\)
(B) Kinetic-theory assumption that fails at very low temperature(ii) \(\text{N m}^4\text{ K}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
(C) Relation between ideal pressure and observed pressure(iii) Volume of gas molecules is negligible compared to container space
(D) SI unit of the quantity \(\frac{pV^2T^2}{n}\)(iv) There is no force of attraction between gas molecules

Choose the correct match from the options given below.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Real gases deviate from ideality because two postulates of the kinetic molecular theory—negligible molecular volume and zero intermolecular attraction—break down at high pressures and low temperatures.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Evaluation
At very high pressures, the space occupied by molecules is no longer negligible compared to the container volume. At very low temperatures, molecules move slowly and intermolecular attractive forces become significant. Because attractive forces reduce the wall impact, the ideal pressure is related to the observed pressure by \(p_{\text{ideal}} = p_{\text{real}} + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\). For the quantity \(\frac{pV^2T^2}{n}\), substituting SI units gives \(\frac{(\text{N m}^{-2})(\text{m}^3)^2(\text{K})^2}{\text{mol}} = \text{N m}^4\text{ K}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.
